stories.title: Government urged to make teaching more attractive
stories.summary: The Teachers' Union of Ireland (TUI) has said that the retention of teachers within the system is now "as big a challenge as initial recruitment". It also said that teachers are being deflected from teaching by ever-increasing administrative duties. The union is pressing the Department of Education to introduce effective measures to retain those teachers who have recently entered the education system. TUI president Anthony Quinn said: "Teachers want to teach, yet it is abundantly clear that they are being distracted from teaching and learning by increasing administrative workload.

stories.summary: The Minister for Justice has warned those driving the wrong way down a motorway: "You'll end up in jail or you'll end up in a grave." Speaking at Government Buildings, Jim O'Callaghan confirmed that gardaí are now to receive pursuit training following the fatal crash on the M9 yesterday. He was speaking after a car, which was carrying five teenage boys, was driven southbound on the northbound carriageway of the motorway when it hit a second car. The five boys were killed and four other people - three women and a seven-year-old boy - were seriously injured.

stories.title: Can Govt hold the line on restoration of excise on fuel?
stories.summary: The Government had hoped that as the deadline looms to begin restoring excise on fuel that the price shock at the pumps would have eased. But the continuing instability in the Middle East has shattered that expectation and the long hot summer has brought further difficulty as smaller crop yields will lead to food prices rising again. This all means that there is serious political pressure on 1 September deadline for the first of four hikes to petrol and diesel. Back in March, the Government signed off on a 'temporary' excise cut to cushion motorists, hauliers and farmers from the increases at the pumps.

stories.title: Search for Indonesia quake victims as thousands displaced
stories.summary: Rescuers in eastern Indonesia are combing through collapsed buildings to find anyone who might still be trapped under rubble after a deadly quake killed at least 68 people and injured 100, as the country marks ⁠its Independence Day reeling from the impact of fresh tremors. Saturday's disaster in the province of East Nusa Tenggara was the country's deadliest since a 2022 quake killed hundreds in West Java. The quake also caused landslides and blocked roads across Indonesia's southernmost province, including the regions of Sikka and Manggarai. Thousands of people displaced by the powerful earthquake in eastern Indonesia awaited aid as they camped out at schools, police stations and government offices.

stories.title: Kobe-mania and the Irish experiment
stories.summary: The AFL's Irish experiment nearly failed before even it really even began - and it all came down to a split-second decision in the 1987 Victorian Football League preliminary final between Melbourne and Hawthorn. The VFL was three years from morphing into the AFL and a huge crowd had gathered to watch what turned into a manic final quarter with tennis legend Pat Cash even interrupting a family holiday to attend. Melbourne missed chance after chance to kill off the Hawks’ challenge in the final minutes of the match, Simon Eishold’s incredible mis-hit hook behind long remembered by Demons fans, but it was the final play that saw it go down in infamy and left recently-recruited Dubliner Jim Stynes labelled as a laughing stock. Kept alive by Melbourne’s inefficiency, Gary Buckenara was given one last chance to win it from Hawthorn but from way out, it was a low percentage chance.

Craig Hansberry's young Connacht side led early on, and twice closed the gap to three points, but they are now a point behind second-placed Leinster, in the table, heading into the final round. stories.title: 100 Buildings: Arresting architecture - Whitehall Garda Station
stories.summary: The former Whitehall Garda Station was built at a time when the young State was redefining itself. It began life as a symbol of a new style of policing. Today, it serves a very different public function as the home of the Dublin City Mortuary and the Office of the State Pathologist. When An Garda Síochána was established in 1923, an extensive Garda station building programme began. This marked the transition from defensive, state-focused Royal Irish Constabulary (RIC) barracks of the 19th century (thick stone walls, high positioned windows) into domestic scale, more accessible, community-focused civic structures. stories.title: Review: 8-year-old puts two smartphone alternatives to the test
stories.summary: As a father of an eight-year-old daughter, my wife and I are beginning to loosen the safety net - just a little. In years gone by, I would have spent my summer holidays out playing from morning to evening without a care in the world until the smell of hot dinners drew us home for the night. However, times have changed, and parents want to know where their kids are when they are out of sight. This creates a dilemma. Eight seems far too young, in my opinion, for a phone that could bring the pitfalls of internet dangers, but old enough to be trusted with a certain degree of independence. So, what devices are out there, if any, that suit the bill? Well, two manufacturers of smart devices – Xplora and Karri - believe that their products can successfully fill an undoubted hole in the market for primary school children, and we were lucky enough to test them out over the past few weeks.

stories.title: Trump threatens Oman if it 'gets in way' of Iran deal
stories.summary: President Donald Trump has threatened to bomb Oman if it "gets in the way" of a US deal with Iran on the Strait of Hormuz and called for Iran to surrender in a war that has become a growing political burden. Control of the waterway, which Iran has effectively closed since the conflict began on 28 February, remains at the heart of the deadlock between Iran and the United States. With whipsawing fuel prices and public opposition to the war weighing on Republicans ahead of November's midterm elections, Mr Trump has faced mounting pressure to end a stalemate that has dragged on for nearly six months. "If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the sh** out of them," Mr Trump told Fox News journalist Trey Yingst, referring to ongoing talks between Oman and Iran on control of the strait, which lies between the two countries.

stories.title: Almost half of Help to Buy applicants get no support
stories.summary: Almost 49,000 people have received financial support from the Government's Help to Buy scheme since July 2020, new figures show. However, the same figures also show that nearly half of people who applied for the help either did not draw down the support or had their applications rejected. New figures published today show that while a total of 48,878 people have received the help over the past six years, this is out of a total of 88,532 who have applied. This means that nearly 40,000 applications have either been rejected or did not result in a home purchase.

stories.title: Oil rises on Iran war stalemate
stories.summary: Oil prices rose today on a lack of progress in diplomatic efforts to resolve the Iran war, though the absence of major supply outages limited gains. Brent crude futures were up 43 cents, or 0.5%, at $88.95 a barrel this afternoon after hitting a session high of $89.68. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 25 cents, or 0.3%, to $82.65 a barrel. Both contracts gained more than 5% last week following attacks on tankers operated by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company in the Strait of Hormuz and on a Saudi Aramco refinery. But Bjarne Schieldrop at SEB Research said that prices were unlikely to move substantially higher unless there was a halt in the current flow of crude out through the Strait of Hormuz at night and/or a closure of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

stories.title: Ebola outbreak in DR Congo deadliest in country's history
stories.summary: The Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo has killed 2,325 people, surpassing the toll from the 2018-2020 outbreak to become the deadliest in the country's history. Congo's public health institute said in its latest ⁠report that confirmed cases had risen to 4,945, including 101 new cases detected in the previous 24 hours. The outbreak, Congo's 17th, was already the biggest in the country's history in terms of number of cases, a milestone reached in late July. The latest government data shows that the total number of deaths has surpassed the 2,299 deaths recorded in Congo's 2018-2020 outbreak, which was previously the country's worst on record.

stories.title: Boehly, Walter in talks to sell Chelsea stakes – reports
stories.summary: Todd Boehly and Mark Walter are in talks to sell their stakes in Chelsea to majority owner Clearlake Capital, according to reports. American billionaire businessmen Boehly and Walter were two of the investors who partnered with Clearlake to buy the west London club from Roman Abramovich in a sale mandated by the United Kingdom government in May 2022. Private equity company Clearlake currently owns 61.5% of the club, with Boehly and Walter carving up the remaining shares with another investor, Hansjorg Wyss. Chelsea chairman Boehly in particular has reportedly been dissatisfied with the direction of the club recently, notably regarding recruitment, head coaches and a potential new stadium plan.

stories.title: Croke Park keen to host annual Premier League friendlies
stories.summary: Croke Park chiefs are keen to make Premier League pre-season friendlies like Wednesday night's clash between Manchester United and Leeds regular events. The match between the long-standing rivals was the first game of soccer to be played at the home of the GAA since 2009, but was seen as a huge success as a sell-out crowd of 75,000 watched Manchester United beat their old rivals on penalties. The only previous times soccer had been played at the venue were between 2007 and 2009 when it served as the temporary home of the Republic of Ireland during the redevelopment of Lansdowne Road. But Peter McKenna, Croke Park’s stadium and commercial director, is keen to change that to find new revenue streams to put into the GAA.

stories.title: Munster advance to interpro final after Ulster crushing
stories.summary: Munster were merciless in their pursuit of tries as they crushed Ulster 62-0 to qualify for the final on 29 August. Two tries each from Beth Buttimer and player-of-the-match Clodagh O'Halloran, adding to Chisom Ugwueru's electric ninth-minute opener, had Munster leading 31-0 at half-time. Matt Brown's side were relentless at times, adding further tries from Katie Corrigan, Emily Lane, stand-in captain Aoife Corey, Alana McInerney, and newcomer Andrea Murphy. Replacement Caitríona Finn tagged on three conversions, helping them to push past the 60-point mark. Munster visit Connacht next Saturday, while Ulster are back in Belfast to host Leinster.

stories.title: Behind the camera: The Healy-Raes: Blood, Sweat & Tears
stories.summary: Film-maker and entrepreneur, Jerry Kennelly, discusses his new documentary on the Kerry political dynasty, 'The Healy-Raes: Blood, Sweat & Tears'. I wouldn't call it a superiority complex, but growing up in Kerry, you know you’re living in a special place, where almost anything can happen. It’s a stunning place to live, with awesome beauty everywhere, from the rolling farmland of North Kerry to the Dingle Peninsula and real treasures like the lakes of Killarney, Caragh Lake, Caherdaniel, and Valentia Island. And then there were the literary giants like John B Keane, Bryan McMahon and Brendan Kennelly whom you would meet and speak to as if they were ordinary people. They were humble giants among men, just like our footballers who brought home Sam Maguire so often that we were truly shocked when they occasionally failed. It’s a place of high standards and even higher expectations. So, it wasn’t considered extraordinary when a man like Jackie Healy-Rae came along. He wore a variety of unusual headgear, ranging from a Russian Ushanka fur hat to colourful tartans. He wore fancy suits and sported an unusual slickdown trademark haircut. Reporters loved him for his turn of phrase. Over chicken soup and sandwiches in our kitchen, my father Padraig, who was founding editor of Kerry’s Eye, performed Jackie speeches, fresh from that morning’s meeting of Kerry County Council, along with the late then Kerryman journalist Michael O’Regan. They loved his turn of phrase – 'rats as big as cats in the town dump’ he declared, embarrassing staff of Kerry County Council who tried to bring reality into the situation. But Jackie played the game. He knew he could dream up magical quotes which would end up in 48-point newspaper headlines.

stories.title: Bonnie Tyler remembered as 'a star, but never a diva'
stories.summary: Bonnie Tyler has been remembered as "a star, but never a diva" at her funeral, which included renditions of some of her biggest hits. Fans applauded and shouted "goodbye" as the singer's white coffin, etched with symbols including a microphone and a treble clef, was carried into Swansea Minster. The coffin was carried to the soundtrack of Tyler's hits If I Sing You a Love Song and It's a Heartache. During the service, Welsh choir Only Men Aloud sang versions of Tyler's biggest hit, Total Eclipse of the Heart, and Bridge Over Troubled Water, by Simon and Garfunkel.

stories.title: Katelyn Cummins: From Rose of Tralee to apprentice electrician
stories.summary: As her time as Rose of Tralee draws to a close, Katelyn Cummins talks to Claire O'Mahony about a year that has given her many unique experiences, the confidence to take her own path, and confirmed her status as the most glamorous apprentice electrician in Ireland "I know who I am now," says Katelyn Cummins, reflecting on the past year, during which she has had more than 240 engagements as the Rose of Tralee, won Dancing with the Stars, travelled across Ireland and overseas, spoken at conferences and worked with organisations including the Jack and Jill Children’s Foundation and Chernobyl Children International. At the age of 21, Katelyn is also preparing to return to the electrician apprenticeship she paused when the opportunities and commitments of the year made continuing her training temporarily impossible. "I don’t think I’ve ever been this busy in my life," she says. "There have been so many people who’ve said to me, 'I think you’re busier than the President of Ireland,’ and I don’t think they’re wrong, to be honest. I’ve actually just been up the walls since the moment I got selected."

stories.title: NTMA to increase Ireland State Savings rates
stories.summary:
The National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) has announced it is increasing the rates that apply to new issues of Ireland State Savings fixed term products with effect from 30 August. Ireland State Savings is the brand name used to describe the range of Irish Government savings products offered by the NTMA to personal savers. It offers Fixed-Term fixed-rate savings products, Prize Bonds and Deposit Accounts. The NTMA said rates across fixed term products are to increase by up to 0.65% (AER).

It added that the variable rates on Post Office Savings Bank (POSB) deposit accounts are to increase by 0.5% (AER) to 1.25%

While the Prize Bond fund is to increase to 1.5 times its current level, with 10,000 prizes expected to be awarded every week.

stories.title: Offaly's All-Ireland winning captain Pádraig Horan dies
stories.summary: Pádraig Horan, who captained Offaly to their first All-Ireland hurling success in 1981, has died at the age of 76 after a long battle with illness. In a lengthy inter-county career which began at the end of the 1960s, Horan was to the fore as the Faithful famously shocked Kilkenny to win a maiden Leinster title in 1980s. Offaly had arrived, with the St Ryangh's clubman adding three more provincial crowns and another Liam MacCarthy success, in 1985, to his collection. His exploits on the field, first as a defender before moving to the full-forward berth, were also recognised when he was named on the All-Star team for '85. As a coach, he managed Offaly to win a National League title in 1991, while four years later he was at the helm when Birr landed All-Ireland senior club honours.
